findings.claim: Every practice question in the unit is set in a form this paper does not use: 21 x '4 marks — Describe Two Features', 26 x '8 marks — Explain Effects', 21 x '8 marks — Explain Significance' and 14 x '16 marks — Period Argument'. Not one of the 84 questions is an interpretation question.
findings.truth: The British depth study on this paper sets four questions worth 40 marks: an 8-mark interpretation question ('How convincing is Interpretation A about...?'), an 8-mark 'Explain what was important about...', an 8-mark 'Write an account of...', and a 16-mark essay on the specified site, which also carries 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. 'Describe two features' is an Edexcel form; 'Explain the significance of' belongs to the thematic study in the other half of this paper.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B table (four questions: interpretation 8, explain 8, account 8, site essay 16) and 2.2 (Paper 2, 2 hours, 84 marks, Section B four compulsory questions)

findings.claim: Twelve exam tips coach the wrong forms — 'For an Explain Effects question', 'For a Describe Two Features question', 'For an Explain Significance question' — and several add claims about what markers reward.
findings.truth: Rewritten for the four forms this paper sets, with the marker claims removed.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B table

findings.claim: Seven invented exam claims inside the article text: 'Examiners flag this confusion every year as a top reason exam answers lose marks' (L3), 'Examiners reward answers that show this interaction' (L6), 'Examiners reward students who follow these consequences' (L7), 'Examiners reward students who weigh all four factors' (L8), 'Examiners reward students who weigh both sides' (L10), 'one of the most common mistakes in Elizabethan exam answers' (L2), and in L9 'The 16-mark essay often invites students to weigh how far Elizabethan England was a Golden Age. Top-band answers...'.
findings.truth: No published source supports any of these. The L9 claim is also wrong about the paper: the 16-mark question is the essay on the specified site.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B table

findings.claim: 'she could not run a kingdom of four million people on her own' — said of the reign from 1558.
findings.truth: England held roughly 3 million people in the 1560s and about 4.1 million by 1601. Lesson 10 teaches the 3-to-4 million rise, so Lesson 2 contradicts it.
findings.evidence: internal (L10 key fact); Wrigley and Schofield population series

findings.claim: 'The historian John Guy has called him the indispensable man of the regime.'
findings.truth: The quotation could not be verified in any source available here. Cecil's indispensability is well attested (A. F. Pollard: 'from 1558 for forty years the biography of Cecil is almost indistinguishable from that of Elizabeth'), so the substance is kept and the quotation marks and attribution removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'William Cecil, 1st Baron Burghley' (historians quoted there do not include this phrase)

findings.claim: 'The historian Wallace MacCaffrey called this her permanent ambiguity.'
findings.truth: The quotation could not be verified. De-attributed; the point about deliberate ambiguity is kept.
findings.evidence: no source found

findings.claim: 'four bad harvests between 1594 and 1598' and 'four bad harvests (1594-1598)'.
findings.truth: The four consecutive failed harvests were those of 1594, 1595, 1596 and 1597. Lesson 10 dates the same run correctly.
findings.evidence: internal (L10); standard harvest series for the 1590s dearth

findings.claim: Essex was 'well-educated and 33 years younger than the queen'.
findings.truth: Essex was born on 10 November 1565, Elizabeth on 7 September 1533 — 32 years between them.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex'

findings.claim: 'on one famous occasion in 1598 he half-drew his sword at her in the Privy Chamber'.
findings.truth: The quarrel (30 June/1 July 1598) was over who should command in Ireland; the queen struck him on the ear first and he then put his hand to his sword. The room is not established in the accounts, so the Privy Chamber claim is dropped and the cause of the row added.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex'

findings.claim: 'About five other ringleaders were also executed.'
findings.truth: Five conspirators were executed in all, of whom four besides Essex: Blount, Danvers, Meyrick and Cuffe. Sir John Davies was condemned and spared.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, "Essex's Rebellion"

findings.claim: 'Roughly 200 Puritan ministers were deprived of their parishes for refusing' (repeated in the conclusion).
findings.truth: Whitgift's Three Articles produced suspensions rather than deprivations; most of those suspended subscribed after negotiation and returned to their parishes.
findings.evidence: standard account of the 1583-84 subscription campaign

findings.claim: The Douai seminary is placed 'in modern Belgium', repeated in a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: Douai is in the Nord department of France; in 1568 it lay in the Spanish Netherlands.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'English College, Douai'

findings.claim: 'Three major Catholic plots between 1571 and 1583 turned on Mary's claim to the throne' — the paragraph then names only two, and the Babington Plot (1586) is called 'the third'.
findings.truth: Two of the three plots fall between 1571 and 1583 (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583); Babington was 1586.
findings.evidence: internal arithmetic; plot dates confirmed in the same lesson's match question

findings.claim: 'In the early hours of 28 July, the English sent eight fireships... The next morning, off Gravelines...'
findings.truth: The fireships went in at around midnight at the end of 28 July and Gravelines was fought on 29 July. As written, the fireships are a day early and Gravelines lands on 29 July only by accident. Lesson 13 states the sequence correctly ('On the night of 28 July').
findings.evidence: internal (L13); standard Old Style chronology of the campaign

findings.claim: Elizabethan consumer goods listed as 'books, clocks, mirrors, sugar, tobacco, and increasingly tea and spices'.
findings.truth: Tea did not reach England until the 1650s. Tobacco and sugar are correct for the period; tea is an anachronism of about seventy years.
findings.evidence: standard date for the arrival of tea in England (first sold in London c.1657)

findings.claim: Three flashcard answers are comma lists that the content validator rejects: '1586, 1594 and 1596-97' (L9), 'Wool, flax and hemp so the able-bodied could be put to work' (L10), 'About £400,000 in gold, silver and jewels' (L11).
findings.truth: One idea per card. Rewritten so each answer carries a single idea or is long enough that the list is illustrative rather than the payload.
findings.evidence: scripts/_validate_content_json.py, validate_flashcards (enumeration rule)

findings.claim: '1594, 1595 and 1596 produced what contemporaries called the four wet years' — three years for four harvests; the flashcard answer reads '1594, 1595, 1596 and 1596-97', which repeats a year.
findings.truth: The run was the harvests of 1594, 1595, 1596 and 1597.
findings.evidence: internal (L4 key fact, once corrected); standard harvest series

findings.claim: 'Each year, parishioners elected two Overseers of the Poor', repeated as 'Each parish elected unpaid Overseers', 'run by elected Overseers', a knowledge-check stem and a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: Under the 1598 and 1601 Acts the churchwardens and up to four substantial householders were nominated as overseers each year by two Justices of the Peace. They were appointed, not elected by parishioners, and there were normally more than two. No knowledge-check answer changes.
findings.evidence: text of the 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor / 1601 Poor Law

findings.claim: Raleigh is 'from 1585 the holder of a royal patent to plant an English colony in North America'.
findings.truth: Elizabeth granted the charter on 25 March 1584; the first colony sailed in 1585.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Roanoke Colony'

findings.claim: 'The Spanish ambassador watched alongside soldiers and sailors' in the public playhouse audience.
findings.truth: Bernardino de Mendoza was expelled in January 1584 (taught in Lesson 7) and no Spanish ambassador returned until after the peace of 1604, which covers almost the whole life of the Elizabethan public playhouses.
findings.evidence: internal (L7); Anglo-Spanish diplomatic break 1584-1604

findings.claim: Stubbes's Anatomy of Abuses (1583) is said to attack plays as 'the schools of vice', quoted in the article, a knowledge-check stem and a flashcard question.
findings.truth: The phrase could not be verified in Stubbes; the famous anti-theatrical title of that kind is Stephen Gosson's The Schoole of Abuse (1579). The attack on the theatre is real, so the substance stays and the quotation marks go. No knowledge-check answer changes.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Philip Stubbes' (no such phrase recorded)

findings.claim: 'Like Acton Burnell three centuries earlier, Kenilworth in the 1570s shows defences repurposed as display'.
findings.truth: Acton Burnell is a specified site for a different British depth study of this board (the reign of Edward I). A student of this option has never met it, and it looks like residue from another unit.
findings.evidence: spec, Section B options list (Norman England / Edward I / Elizabethan England / Restoration England)

findings.claim: 'a figure of a thousand pounds a day was bandied about, and even if gossip inflated it, the true cost would have crushed most noble families'.
findings.truth: The £1,000 a day figure is contemporary gossip. Estimates of what Leicester actually recorded spending on the 1575 visit are far lower, so the sentence should not build a claim about the true cost on top of the rumour.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Kenilworth Castle' (recorded cost estimate) / English Heritage site history

findings.claim: The lessons state that the Armada campaign is the specified site for 2027 and Kenilworth for 2028.
findings.truth: The spec does not name sites: it says only that the specified site changes annually and is published three years ahead on the board's website. The claims cannot be checked against the spec, so they rest on whatever list the build used. Worth confirming against the board's published site list before the 2027 cohort.
findings.evidence: spec, Part four: 'For all series the specified site will be published three years in advance'

findings.claim: Lesson 8 gives the Armada 19,000 soldiers; Lesson 13 gives 'perhaps eighteen thousand'.
findings.truth: Both are within the usual range for the same fleet, but the unit contradicts itself by a thousand men.
findings.evidence: internal

findings.claim: 'The Levant Company (1581) opened trade with the Ottoman Empire.'
findings.truth: The 1581 charter created the Turkey Company; it merged with the Venice Company in 1592 to become the Levant Company. The 1581 date is normal textbook shorthand and costs no marks.
findings.evidence: standard company chronology

findings.claim: 'A typical company had around twelve sharers.'
findings.truth: The Lord Chamberlain's Men had eight sharers in 1594; a dozen is nearer the King's Men after 1603.
findings.evidence: standard company records

findings.claim: The Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 is described as 'a small attempted uprising by a few dozen poor men'.
findings.truth: The conspiracy involved about twenty men and only a handful turned out on the night. 'A few dozen' overstates it, though the point (a warning rather than a real rising) stands.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of the Enslow Hill rising

findings.claim: 'A 1574 statute... restricted purple silk and cloth-of-gold to the royal family and the highest nobility.'
findings.truth: The 1574 dress rules were issued as a royal proclamation (the Statutes of Apparel), not an Act of Parliament. The exam tip and one practice question now say 'rules on apparel'; the article still says statute.
findings.evidence: 1574 Statutes of Apparel, issued by proclamation

summary: The history is in good order — dates, names and figures are almost all right, and the two historic-environment lessons are strong. The exam scaffolding is not: all 84 practice questions, and the exam tips that go with them, are built on question forms this paper does not set, and no lesson practised the interpretation question that opens every real paper. All 84 questions are rebuilt into the four real forms. Beyond that: seven invented examiner claims, one anachronism (tea), a Belgian Douai, Essex's age and the number executed with him, Raleigh's patent year, two unverifiable historian quotations, an unverifiable Stubbes quotation, a stray Acton Burnell reference from another option, and a handful of counting slips.
